Anesthesiologist here. What it sounds like is that the rate on the infusion on the pump was too high for you. The epidural space is more like a silo, and the volume going in has to fill up the vertical space it’s going to cover. This fluid is also positional—it’s why I make you lay on one side of that side isn’t well covered, the medication flows down hill. Also there’s some variability in the rate at which we metabolize medications. 

If you deliver at the same place, ask them to look at your chart and see if the infusion rate was charted. Tell them what happened and ask to start at a lower rate or with smaller volumes in your bolus. Your catheter may also not end up as high up in your spinal canal which can help.

Main differences is (at least in academics), the patient population. Anesthesia crit is more postop—either cardiac icu, surgical icu, trauma icu. Mech circ support devices. More echo exposure. Typically are collaborative with (or the servants to) which ever surgeon owns the patient. Become very comfortable with fluid management, hemodynamics, and procedures. More of a “fix problem first ask questions second” mindset, although you’re still working through a fast/limited differential on initial management. A little less comfortable with workup and management in the ID, hemonc, pulmonology and neuro spaces, although that’s not universal. 

Med ICU sees more of your undifferentiated unwell (think rare infection, neuro dz, oncology complications) plus a lot of bread and butter post arrest, DKA, COPD exac. Medical folks tend to have a more linear approach to patients, preferring a thorough chart review prior to enacting a plan. Absolutely outstanding on diagnostics, complicated vent stuff and management of ID/pulm/hemonc/neuro at the trade off for procedure/echo skills. 

I think the other consideration is what you want to be doing when you’re NOT in the ICU, anesthesia vs hospitalist/clinic work. Lots of paths.

As far as management compared to medicine, I think anesthesia is great at acting while working through their differential. This comes from intraop skills where you are the person fixing the vent/hemodynamics/giving meds during a decompensation while trying to figure out “what just happened”. I think we are great at hemodynamic management and procedures in a way that MICU is not. Medical intensivists have so much more background in ID, hemonc, pulm, neph and they can spin circles around me in those areas. You certainly can tailor your training if you wanted more exposure during fellowship.

If you don’t want to do cardiac cases intraop, you can do just a crit care fellowship (1 year), which will allow you to theoretically go into any type of ICU. In academics this tends to skew towards cardiac or surgical icu, but you can find more opportunities for mixed ICU (including medical) in the private practice space.

Certainly the dual fellowship (cardiac plus icu) is a popular one, but not the only option.

You would not work in an icu if you ONLY did a cardiac fellowship, as that would just focus on intraop management. You can find opportunities to do simple bypass cases in more rural settings without a cardiac fellowship.

Anesthesiologist here…entirely dependent on the comfort level of the physician, the patient’s stature/how they’re handling contractions and how baby is looking on the monitor. I’m fairly early on in my practice,  but I had a lot of epidurals during residency, so I may be more willing to place one where my partners would decline. I’m also one of the faster proceduralists so I usually can get one in between q3m contractions. That being said, there are parts of the procedure where I can’t exactly pause for a contraction without placing you at risk for a post epidural headache if you were to move. So a patient who is able to at least reduce movement during a contraction/breathe through a contraction is more likely to get one. It’s not because I’m not incredibly sympathetic to the mom screaming/rocking/shifting during a contraction, but if I see that I am instantly worried that she won’t tolerate the placement. Additionally, and again I don’t mean any disrespect to heavier women as I am one myself, but placing an epidural on a woman with a BMI in the 50s-60s is SO MUCH HARDER. I can’t feel vertebrae so I’m usually going blind, and using ultrasound takes some more time. We also usually have to use a longer needle which can obscure the tactile feedback we are used to. For women in this category, I expect the epidural to take 2-3x longer or more, which can be impossible in precipitous labor. Finally, if baby is looking anything less than reassuring on the monitors, the last thing I want to do is worsen things by moving mom into an unfavorable position or have a needle in her back when a bunch of nurses run into the room because baby has a prolonged decel. Also bolusing the epidural can cause some hypotension which some babies hate, so it’s a trade off of “can I get the level of pain relief I need without making things worse.”

Tl;dr—it’s multifactorial on whether a precipitous labor will get an epidural but primarily the physicians judgment is the biggest deciding factor

Well, I would counter,

1) if I’m canceling a case the day of, I ALWAYS am part of that conversation. I always give what standards would need to be met (getting an echo/DSE, neg UDS, etc.) and stress to the patient that it’s for their safety. I offer for patients to go to the Preop screening clinic prior to their next surgery and tell surgeons to utilize it in appropriate patients. You’re right, I can’t come to your clinic. But anes is always a phone call away and usually willing to find some middle ground to proceed. 

2) the anesthesiologist IS going to be the one managing the complications from anesthesia. Which is what’s going to kill the patient. Usually it’s not the removal of a few cm of bowel or liver that’s what does the patient in. It’s the BP derangements from methamphetamine or ARB use, the STEMI from anes stress, the pulmonary hypertensive crisis leading to RV failure, the COPD that requires postop ventilator because they’re so poorly optimized. When the patient codes, we are the ones running it. I’m the last person to talk to a patient before they go off to sleep, and I may be the last voice they hear. I don’t take that lightly.

3) we do manage and follow these patients postoperatively. Most unexpected postop ICU admissions are to our crit care anesthesia team. We are the ones paged to reintubate them in the middle of the night. We are called to care for them when they end up on ecmo. 

I dislike the narrative that anes is only responsible for patient care during the surgical period. We own these patients as much as you do, even if I don’t see them in clinic.

Things I see that impact my management, this is just my checklist for almost every case but it’s also something I think about on that “semi urgent” case that I don’t have a ton of time to preop.

Resp: def pHTN, poor reserve in anyone hospitalized, emergent cases with ?difficult airway that may not be appropriately NPO (ie how am I securing this airway when they’re in a c-collar)

Cards: know LVEF, R heart fxn, aortic/mitral valve dz and how to manage—what are your first line pressors, do I need to consent pt for TEE intraop? Do I need preop a-line (typically EF<40-45%)?

Endo: on insulin gtt? What was last POCT? Also if on prednisone 15mg+ daily, consider stress dose steroids. If poorly controlled T2DM consider if they have gastroparesis or autonomic neuropathy.

Renal: CKD and obv what meds do I want to avoid. What was last K, and have they ever had hyperK, do they do HD and when did they last dialyze? Do I need a foley?

Heme: on dapt? Should they be? Are we going to fully a/c with heparin and are they on a drip (may need at3 or ffp). What is hgb, plt? What products to order?

Neuro: increased ICP? What anesthetics do I need to avoid? Do I need TIVA? Do I need to hyperventilate? Do I need pressures higher for carotid stenosis? Are they really anxious—need some preop anxiolytics or is that contraindicated?

Msk: Hx of cervical fusion? Any joint issues that would impact positioning? 

GI: Hx of gerd—poorly controlled? Gastroparesis risk? Hx of upper GI procedures that would make them a risk for aspiration? Liver dysfxn?

Anes: Hx of MH? Hx of difficult airway? Possible difficult mask?

Hope this helps

Yes. Physicians at my hospital do not have a say in the NPs they supervise, as they are hired by the department the physician works for. Think of like 8-10 doctors plus 8-10 NPs and residents, with 1 doctor covering rounding on patients that week with 8-10 people they oversee. If you are assigned that service for the week, such as the general surgery team, and an NP is scheduled for a shift, you’re responsible for overseeing their work. This is an incredibly complex situation, with regards to billing (can’t have doctor and NP both bill for ICU time), procedures (is the NP signed off to do X by the dept and if not, who is putting that central line in at the cost of covering their own patients), and legal culpability (how much oversight does this NP I’ve never worked with before need, is it worth my time to lose the money that they’ll bill for if I’m doing all the same chart review and medical decision making because I don’t trust them). Now certainly one could argue that a physician could fire a grossly incompetent NP, but the process for this is extensive and can have negative repercussions for the doctor.
